To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the human grasp postposes can be categorized based on their functional relation to the object shape, size, or task.
we trained a 400 unit SOM to analyze and visualize human grasp postures captured during imagined grasping.

we trained a SOM to visualize the dimensionality of the hand posture during imagined grasping, we showed clear boundaries between the clusters of grasp postures and we quantified the functional relations between the grasp posture and the object shape.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new approach to grasp analysis, and the application of this approach to the analysis of human grasping.
developing an understanding of how human grasping is related to the object shape, and the functional role of the grasp.
the development of new computational tools for the analysis of grasping and the development of a new grasp taxonomy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our approach provides an effective way of analyzing and visualizing human grasping behavior and can potentially be applied to design adaptive grasp planning algorithms for robot hands.
the SOM is an effective tool for grasping classification and analysis.
the grasp taxonomy based on qualitative observation of the human grasping behavior can be quantitatively verified and extended by analyzing human grasp postures captured during imagined grasping.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the grasp postures can be clustered into functional groups and the boundaries between these functional groups are related to the joints with high covariance.
the human hand is able to reduce the complexity of grasping to a few degrees of freedom, which is a key to understanding how the hand works and to designing robotic hand.
the human grasps are highly redundant, but they can be classified in a low dimensional manifold, which can be used to design adaptive grasping algorithm for robotic hands.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the human grasp posture can be classified in a low dimensional feature space.
the SOM is a powerful tool for analyzing the dimensionality reduction of the hand posture and for clustering the grasps.
we can use a simple clustering algorithm to visualize the structure of the human hand grasping space and to identify the joint groups that are most correlated with the object shape.
